notes.text: Upon me — Though the prophet may speak of himself, yet it is principally to be understood of Christ. Anointed - Set me apart, both capacitating him with gifts, and commissioning him with authority; and yet more, as it is applied to Christ, a power to make all effectual, from whence he hath also the name of Messiah among the Hebrew, and of Christ among the Greeks; nay, Christ alone among the prophets hath obtained this name, Psalm xlv, 7. The prophet describes first, who Christ is, and then what are his offices. Liberty - This appertains to Christ's kingly office, whereby he proclaims liberty from the dominion of sin, and from the fear of hell.

Vengeance — It being necessary, that where God will deliver his people, he should take vengeance on their enemies; principally on the enemies of his church, and the spiritual ones chiefly, Satan, sin, and death.

Ashes — By ashes understand whatever is proper for days of mourning, as by beauty whatever may become times of rejoicing. Oil of joy - He calls it oil of joy in allusion to those anointings they were wont to use in times of joy, gladness for heaviness; and it is called a garment in allusion to their festival ornaments, for they had garments appropriated to their conditions, some suitable to times of rejoicing, and some to times of mourning. Called - That they may be so. Trees - That they shall be firm, solid, and well rooted, being by faith engrafted into Christ, and bringing forth fruit suitable to the soil wherein they are planted.

Love judgment — I will do them right, for I love justice in myself, and in them that practice it. Robbery - All things gotten by injustice, though it be for sacrifice. Direct - I will lead them so, that they shall do all things in sincerity. Everlasting covenant - Though you have broken covenant with me, yet I will renew my ancient covenant made with your fathers, confirmed with the blood of Christ, and it shall be everlasting, never to be abrogated.

Shall be — That is, eminently a promise of the increase of the church; such shall be their prosperity, and multiplying, that they shall be known abroad by their great increase; or else, the meaning is, the church shall have a seed of the Gentiles, whereas the church has been confined to one corner of the world, now it shall remain in one nation alone no more, but shall fill all the nations of the earth. Hath blessed - There shall be such visible characters of God's love to them, and of God's grace in them.
I will — This is spoken in the person of the church. Garments, &c. - With salvation as with a garment, and with righteousness as with a robe.

Righteousness — His great work of salvation shall break out and appear. Praise - As the natural product, and fruit of it. A prayer of the watchmen for the church in confidence of God's gracious designs and promises to it, ver. 1-12.

glossa.text:
*The Spirit of the Lord* ((HIER.)) Christ according to the humanity, who had said above, *I the Lord, in the time will gather them,* etc.

*Because he hath anointed me:* with the oil of gladness, with the abundance of grace. ((ID.)) This anointing was completed in the baptism, because the Spirit of the Lord descended in the likeness of a dove, and remained upon him.

*To announce.* The Seventy: To preach the Gospel to the poor.

*An opening,* namely a loosing; for thus Symmachus more openly rendered it.
*The day of vengeance:* ((ID.)) of damnation, which came through the Romans, according to that: *The day shall come,* etc. And, *when you shall see Jerusalem compassed about with an army,* etc.

*A crown.* When, that is, they shall have seen that very many of the Jews have believed, and that they receive a most clean robe for a mourning garment.

*For ashes.* For the grief and sorrow of their own fruits, when, that is, they shall have seen the Gentiles flowing together to the faith, they shall have the oil of joy for mourning, the mantle of praise for the spirit of grief.

*For I am the Lord:* As though he said: This shall the Lord do, who loves rather the justice of the poor and true judgment than the gifts of the rich, which are often from rapine; nor do they please him more than the hire of a harlot, or the price of flesh in sacrifice, or if a man should immolate his son to the Lord.

*In truth.* That they may eat the lamb in truth, that they may make the circumcision of the heart, and do in truth all the things that were given in figure.

*An everlasting covenant.* The eternal Gospel, not as the Old Testament, which the Gospel succeeds.
*Their seed.* The faithful, to whom the apostles committed the seed of the word which they received from the Lord.

*Rejoicing I will rejoice* in the Lord, not in the world.

*With the garments of salvation:* with the virtues, with Christ himself, etc., *as far as* yet the Church is one in the head and in the members.

*And as a bride.* He sets forth the examples of another comparison, of which the former is referred to the bridegroom, the latter to the bride.
*And praise:* his own, etc., *as far as* he shall render to the Lord the fruit of praise and of good working.

notes.text: Turned — Brought the captive Israelites out of Babylon into their own land. Dream - We were so surprized and astonished.

Turn — As thou hast brought us home, bring also the rest of our brethren. As - As thou art pleased sometimes to send floods of water into dry and barren grounds, such as the southern parts of Canaan were. We must trust in God for success in all enterprizes, ver. 1, 2. And for children, ver. 3-5. A song of degrees of Solomon.

glossa.text: *A canticle of degrees.* ((CASS.)) The seventh degree, in a figure of the Old Testament, prophesies through Christ who is to come the return from captivity, as it were from Babylon: whence now consolation, and a sowing that more may be reaped. ((AUG.)) Those redeemed by the blood of Christ and turned back from captivity sing these things, while they are pilgrims, groaning by the way. Sion is Jerusalem, eternal in the angels, captive in men. *In the turning.* ((CASS.)) First the greatness of the deed is shown, with the greatness of the joy: secondly he prays for the turning from captivity still to come, there, *Turn again, O Lord. In the turning.* ((AUG.)) Or, when he shall have turned, etc., *as far as turn again, O Lord, our captivity. As.* ((ID.)) It is not always set for a likeness, but for a property, as here; whence it is also said: He did as a just man, which he truly is; so these are made *as men comforted,* that is, they rejoiced, as receiving consolation in the resurrection of Christ, who went before that we might follow.

*Our mouth.* ((CASS.)) The secret of the heart, where joys first are, which afterwards break forth by the office of the tongue. ((AUG.)) *Our mouth.* Of the heart: thence proceeds the evil and the good which cleanses or defiles us; whence not: *That which proceedeth out of the mouth, defileth ((Marc. VII))* . Not of the mouth of the flesh, but of the heart. For thou art not unclean if thou namest thefts and other evils: but while thou thinkest of them, even if thou keep silence. *Among the Gentiles.* ((ID.)) Not the Gentiles, because not all believe. *He hath magnified,* because they see them work miracles also; a firm testimony from an adversary. ((CASS.)) And he has truly magnified, lest thou doubt because of the words of the Gentiles.

*Turn again, O Lord.* ((ID.)) The second part. He prays for the turning which is to come, in which there shall be a sowing in hope of joy. ((ID.)) The redemption of the coming of the Lord having been foretold, they pray again that their own sins be forgiven. In the general remission they rejoice, and they pray pardon for themselves. *Turn again, O Lord, our captivity.* ((ID.)) There was none according to the letter in the days of David, but under the devil the world was captive, etc., *as far as* it is not therefore to be given over, because *he that soweth in tears.* ((THEOD.)) He calls Jerusalem the south, etc., *as far as* that they may be constrained, and make their way after the manner of a torrent.

*In tears.* ((AUG.)) Spiritual sowing is always in tears, whence: *Blessed are they that mourn.* But they who sow in the flesh, sow with gladness: but afterwards weeping: because *mourning taketh hold of the end of joy.* ((ID.)) Zacchaeus, *Behold the half,* etc., *as far as: He that shall give a cup of cold water shall not lose his reward ((Matth. X))*.

*Going.* ((CASS.)) By the advancement of a better life. *Casting,* sending on before them into that world. *Their own,* not of rapine, but of their own labour; *coming,* to the judgment. This is common to all, but to joy none come but the good. *And they wept.* ((AUG.)) Because they were wretched, etc., *as far as* he wishes that many be sick.

notes.text: Rejoice evermore — In uninterrupted happiness in God. Pray without ceasing - Which is the fruit of always rejoicing in the Lord. In everything give thanks - Which is the fruit of both the former. This is Christian perfection. Further than this we cannot go; and we need not stop short of it. Our Lord has purchased joy, as well as righteousness, for us. It is the very design of the gospel that, being saved from guilt, we should be happy in the love of Christ. Prayer may be said to be the breath of our spiritual life. He that lives cannot possibly cease breathing. So much as we really enjoy of the presence of God, so much prayer and praise do we offer up without ceasing; else our rejoicing is but delusion. Thanksgiving is inseparable from true prayer: it is almost essentially connected with it. He that always prays is ever giving praise, whether in ease or pain, both for prosperity and for the greatest adversity. He blesses God for all things, looks on them as coming from him, and receives them only for his sake; not choosing nor refusing, liking nor disliking, anything, but only as it is agreeable or disagreeable to his perfect will.
For this — That you should thus rejoice, pray, give thanks. Is the will of God - Always good, always pointing at our salvation.

Quench not the Spirit — Wherever it is, it burns; it flames in holy love, in joy, prayer, thanksgiving. O quench it not, damp it not in yourself or others, either by neglecting to do good, or by doing evil!

Despise not prophesyings — That is, preaching; for the apostle is not here speaking of extraordinary gifts. It seems, one means of grace is put for all; and whoever despises any of these, under whatever pretense, will surely (though perhaps gradually and almost insensibly) quench the Spirit.

Meantime, prove all things — Which any preacher recommends. (He speaks of practice, not of doctrines.) Try every advice by the touchstone of scripture, and hold fast that which is good - Zealously, resolutely, diligently practice it, in spite of all opposition.

And be equally zealous and careful to abstain from all appearance of evil — Observe, those who "heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears," under pretense of proving all things, have no countenance or excuse from this scripture.

And may the God of peace sanctify you — By the peace he works in you, which is a great means of sanctification. Wholly - The word signifies wholly and perfectly; every part and all that concerns you; all that is of or about you. And may the whole of you, the spirit and the soul and the body - Just before he said you; now he denominates them from their spiritual state. The spirit - Gal. vi, 8; wishing that it may be preserved whole and entire: then from their natural state, the soul and the body; (for these two make up the whole nature of man, Matt. x, 28;) wishing it may be preserved blameless till the coming of Christ. To explain this a little further: of the three here mentioned, only the two last are the natural constituent parts of man. The first is adventitious, and the supernatural gift of God, to be found in Christians only. That man cannot possibly consist of three parts, appears hence: The soul is either matter or not matter: there is no medium. But if it is matter, it is part of the body: if not matter, it coincides with the Spirit.
Who also will do it — Unless you quench the Spirit.

glossa.text: *In Christ.* The will of God has been shown, because these things were in Christ, in whom nothing displeased God. *Extinguish not the Spirit.* Because it is the will of God to do all these things, you who are greater, who have through the Holy Spirit the gift of understanding, hide it not, by which desert you also would lose it. You subjects, despise not their prophecies; nevertheless receive not all things indiscriminately, but *prove* them, that is, examine them by reason, and hold what is found good. *Extinguish not the Spirit,* that is: If the Holy Spirit reveals anything to anyone's ear, forbid thou him not to speak what he perceives. The Holy Spirit who has been given to us we extinguish, not as to what is in himself, but in us, when by sinning we put him to flight.

*And may the God of peace himself sanctify you in all things,* etc. That is, I thus admonish prelates and subjects, but God himself is he who is able. *Your spirit.* Let the reason be kept entire, by not consenting to the flesh. *And soul.* That is, let the sensuality be kept entire, by serving the reason. *And body.* That you do nothing by its ministry. Whence anyone may complain. Sometimes the soul is defiled by an evil thought and yet the body is clean. And therefore he says that the spirit ought to be entire in man. But if an evil life, or an evil thought, intervene, there will not be spirit. Spirit and soul and body, of which man consists, namely that by which we understand, and that by which we live, and that by which we are visible and palpable, which again are called two, because often the soul is named together with the spirit. *Without complaint.* It is one thing to be without sin, which in this life was said of the Only-begotten alone. It is another to be without complaint, which could be said of many just men even in this life. For there is a certain manner of good life, of which even in this present conversation there could be no just complaint. *In the coming.* That is, even unto the end of life.

*Faithful.* As if he should say: I pray that he may sanctify, that he may keep you sanctified; nor is there to be any doubt thereof, because he is true in his promises, who called you to this, that you should be holy.

notes.text: There was a man — The evangelist now proceeds to him who testified of the light, which he had spoken of in the five preceding verses.

The same came for (that is, in order to give) a testimony — The evangelist, with the most strong and tender affection, interweaves his own testimony with that of John, by noble digressions, wherein he explains the office of the Baptist; partly premises and partly subjoins a further explication to his short sentences. What St. Matthew, Mark, and Luke term the Gospel, in respect of the promise going before, St. John usually terms the testimony, intimating the certain knowledge of the relator; to testify of the light - Of Christ.
The Jews — Probably the great council sent.
I am not the Christ — For many supposed he was.
Art thou Elijah? — He was not that Elijah (the Tishbite) of whom they spoke. Art thou the prophet - Of whom Moses speaks, Deut. xviii, 15.

He said — I am that forerunner of Christ of whom Isaiah speaks. I am the voice - As if he had said, Far from being Christ, or even Elijah, I am nothing but a voice: a sound that so soon as it has expressed the thought of which it is the sign, dies into air, and is known no more. Isaiah xl, 3.

They who were sent were of the Pharisees — Who were peculiarly tenacious of old customs, and jealous of any innovation (except those brought in by their own scribes) unless the innovator had unquestionable proofs of Divine authority.
They asked him, Why baptizest thou then? — Without any commission from the sanhedrim? And not only heathens (who were always baptized before they were admitted to circumcision) but Jews also?

John answered, I baptize — To prepare for the Messiah; and indeed to show that Jews, as well as Gentiles, must be proselytes to Christ, and that these as well as those stand in need of being washed from their sins.
Where John was baptizing — That is, used to baptize.

glossa.text: *There was a man sent.* After he had ascended by a lofty flight beyond every nature into the height of theology, because he had contemplated that the Word had always been with the Father, he presently descends to the lowliness of human nature, and particularly of the Word's forerunner, against those who said that human nature had been in the first parent wholly lost and brought to nothing. *A man sent.* A man, not an angel, as the heretics will have it, sent from God. Therefore he was able to speak of God.

*And this.* Both this and the other testimonies of John that follow were given after Christ had been baptized, when Jesus was now coming to invite the disciples, whom John by his testimonies sends to him. A testimony against this, that Christ was hidden: hidden, because lowly; lowly, that he might be able to be despised and killed, that he might redeem the world. *Who art thou.* The Jews thought John to be the Christ who was promised in the law. Others thought him to be Elias, because of his exceeding abstinence and chastity, and his solitary life, and his most sharp rebuking of offences, and the most severe terror of the vengeance to come. Others said that he was one of the prophets raised up again, because of the grace of prophecy.

*He confessed.* He confessed, as he says afterwards, not that he was the Christ. He did not deny what he was, that is, that he was the forerunner, as he says when questioned afterwards: *I am the voice of one crying.* The order of the words is: and he confessed and did not deny, when they sent.

*Art thou Elias?* Since all knew the name of Christ, they knew also that Elias was to go before him. But Elias himself is to go before him as about to judge in power; John is figuratively Elias, going before the same one as about to be judged: so that there are two heralds, as there are two advents of the same one. Whence: *I am not Elias,* that is, not the herald pointing to his power; but I show the lowliness at which you take offence. As if he should say: Serve the lowly one before the exalted one judges. Behold, neither am I the Christ, nor a judge on the side of power.

*I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness.* He does not say, I am a man, or John, or the son of Zacharias. He does not regard his human subsistence or his generation, but, exalted beyond all these things as the forerunner of the Word, he forsakes all things that are contained within the world. He ascends on high, made the voice of the Word, and confesses in himself no substance beyond the abundance of grace by which he surpasses every creature, that he may be the voice of the Word. The voice is the interpreter of the mind; but the mind, that is, the understanding of all things, is the Son of God. John therefore is the voice and interpreter of this mind, because he first showed him to the world: *Behold the Lamb of God. Isaias,* prophesied this of John: *I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness,* in which the word sounds, that is, prophecy, and the showing forth and the lamp of the Word present.

*Of the Pharisees.* That is, of the chief men of the Jews, who do not seek doctrine, but envy it. Who nevertheless come to John for this reason, that they hear that he has preached the common resurrection of all, which they themselves also believed; whence they themselves also agree with Christ in many things. They gave hearing to the Apostle Paul also in many things.

*Why then dost thou baptize.* The Pharisees heard in the prophets that Christ would come and would baptize, knowing that the Jordan had borne the figure of baptism, and that Elias and Eliseus had crossed it with dry feet; and they did not doubt that the figure of baptism had gone before in Elias and Eliseus, whence they now thought that these had risen again and had baptized. Whence they do not ask, Art thou one of the prophets? but only: Art thou the prophet? that one, namely, who prefigured baptism.

*I baptize in water.* Let not what I do be imputed to boldness, because I wash bodies with water, I do not take away sins; so that, as I am forerunner in being born and in preaching, so also in baptizing: but he is in the midst of you who takes away sins.

*Whose I am not worthy,* etc. He does not say, I will not loose. For he does loose, since he made him manifest and disclosed many things concerning his divinity and his humanity; but, I am not worthy, because he reckons himself unworthy for the doing of this, in which humility is simply shown.

*These things in Bethania.* There are two Bethanias. One beyond the Jordan, the other round about, not far from Jerusalem, where Lazarus was raised. That which is beyond the Jordan signifies human nature under the natural law before the streams of grace, which grace was abundant after the incarnation of Christ; which nature had been created to this end, that it should obey the law of nature, in which John baptizes, because he does not free from sin. He baptizes beyond the streams of the divine gifts, which had not yet begun in Christ to descend into human nature. That which is on this side of the Jordan signifies the same human nature obedient under the law of grace, which is nearest to Jerusalem, that is, to the vision of peace, through charity, in which Christ raises the dead man, because he frees from sin.

The Lord has done great things for us
I will give you as a light to the nations

echoes.text: Let us choose for us that which is right. Let us know among ourselves what is good.
echoes.note: Elihu's 'Let us choose for ourselves that which is right; let us know among ourselves what is good' offers a faint sapiential parallel to Paul's 'Test all things, and hold firmly that which is good' (5:21), the discernment of good from its counterfeit.

echoes.text: Doesn’t the ear try words, even as the palate tastes its food?
echoes.note: 'Doesn't the ear try words, even as the palate tastes its food?' supplies a testing/discernment image akin to Paul's command to test everything (5:21). Faint and figural.

echoes.text: Oh taste and see that Yahweh is good. Blessed is the man who takes refuge in him.
echoes.note: 'Taste and see that the LORD is good' parallels the discern-the-good motif of 'Test all things, and hold firmly that which is good' (5:21). Faint and contested.

echoes.text: Hate evil, love good, and establish justice in the courts. It may be that Yahweh, the God of Armies, will be gracious to the remnant of Joseph.”
echoes.note: 'Hate the evil, love the good' parallels Paul's paired commands to 'hold firmly that which is good' and 'abstain from every form of evil' (5:21-22). A faint prophetic-ethical backdrop.

echoes.text: You who love Yahweh, hate evil. He preserves the souls of his saints. He delivers them out of the hand of the wicked.
echoes.note: 'You who love the LORD, hate evil' resonates with the good/evil antithesis of 'hold firmly that which is good... abstain from every form of evil' (5:21-22). Faint.

echoes.text: I will bless Yahweh at all times. His praise will always be in my mouth.
echoes.note: 'I will bless the LORD at all times; his praise shall continually be in my mouth' offers a faint backdrop to the continual praise and thanksgiving commanded in 'Rejoice always... In everything give thanks' (5:16-18). Faint and contested.

echoes.text: Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
echoes.note: The prayer that the believer's 'whole spirit, soul, and body' be preserved blameless (5:23) reflects an anthropology rooted in Genesis, where God breathes the breath of life into the body so that the man becomes a living soul. Faint and figural.

echoes.text: You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.
echoes.note: The Shema's command to love God with heart, soul, and might gives a faint background to Paul's whole-person sanctification of 'spirit, soul, and body' (5:23). Contested as a verbal source.

echoes.text: Then Gideon built an altar there to Yahweh, and called it “Yahweh is Peace.” To this day it is still in Ophrah of the Abiezrites.
echoes.note: The divine title 'the God of peace' (5:23) draws on Israel's covenantal naming of God with peace, as where Gideon names the altar 'The LORD is Peace.' A faint backdrop to Paul's recurring peace-of-God title.

echoes.text: ‘Yahweh bless you, and keep you. Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.’
echoes.note: The Aaronic blessing's climactic gift of peace ('the LORD... give you peace') stands faintly behind the benedictory 'God of peace' and the wish for blameless preservation in the closing prayer (5:23). Faint and figural.

echoes.text: Know therefore that Yahweh your God himself is God, the faithful God, who keeps covenant and loving kindness with them who love him and keep his commandments to a thousand generations,
echoes.note: 'Know therefore that the LORD your God... is the faithful God' undergirds Paul's assurance 'He who calls you is faithful' (5:24). A faint covenantal echo of God's reliability to fulfill his word.

echoes.text: The Rock, his work is perfect, for all his ways are just. A God of faithfulness who does no wrong, just and right is he.
echoes.note: 'A God of faithfulness who does no wrong' resonates with 'He who calls you is faithful, who will also do it' (5:24). Faint and one of several covenant-faithfulness texts.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, behold, he comes!” says Yahweh of Armies.
echoes.note: 'Behold, I send my messenger' frames John as the divinely sent forerunner ('there came a man, sent from God'). The sending-of-the-messenger motif is the standard prophetic preparation pattern and coheres with John's witness role; medium because the verbal link is conceptual.

echoes.text: yes, he says, “It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give you for a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.”
echoes.note: 'A light to the nations' resonates with 'the true light that enlightens everyone' (v.9), the universal scope of illumination. Low confidence: the universalizing of light is a shared Isaianic theme rather than a direct quotation.

echoes.text: Yahweh is my light and my salvation. Whom shall I fear? Yahweh is the strength of my life. Of whom shall I be afraid?
echoes.note: 'The LORD is my light and my salvation' supplies the divine-light identification that the Prologue transfers to the Logos. Faint and contested; included for recurrence of the light-as-God motif.

harmony.title: The Word made flesh
harmony.note: John alone begins before time itself — "In the beginning was the Word" — where the others begin with a birth or a baptism.

registers.label: Spare
lines: The Spirit of the Lord is upon us.
Good news for the poor, release for the captive.
Those who went out weeping, carrying seed—
come home with shouts of joy.
A man came, sent from God, to point to the light.
We are not the light; we testify to it.
Come, let us worship with mouths full of laughter.
Come, Lord Jesus. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: When the Lord turned our captivity, we were like those who dream — our mouths filled with laughter, our tongues with shouts of joy.
Come, Lord Jesus, come.
He has clothed us with the garment of praise, traded ashes for a garland, mourning for the oil of gladness.
Come, Lord Jesus, come.
So we who went out weeping, carrying our small handful of seed, come home with our arms full of sheaves.
Come, Lord Jesus, come.
Rejoice always; the One who calls you is faithful. Come, point to the light with us.
Come, Lord Jesus, come. Amen.

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: The Spirit anoints us with the oil of gladness.
Come, Lord Jesus, come.
Ashes are traded for a garland of joy.
Come, Lord Jesus, come.
We sow in tears and come home singing.
Come, Lord Jesus, come.
Come, let us worship and point to the light.
Come, Lord Jesus, come. Amen.
